extracted.intended_audience: NPR listeners, public editor readers, and broadcast journalists/newscast staff interested in how NPR newscasts are produced and selected
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting, scheduling, producing, and editing short NPR newscasts (hourly 5-minute broadcasts), including roles, timing, sourcing, fairness, repetition, and correction practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchors write and engineer their own scripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes, the anchors write their own scripts and read them on the air, and they also engineer the broadcast by themselves (meaning they don't have someone in the recording booth pressing buttons for them or managing their volume levels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other roles on the shift include a producer (leader who mostly decides what stories will run), an editor (fact-checks and edits scripts and correspondent reports), and an associate producer (edits audio). Anchors therefore must be skilled both at writing concise copy and operating the board/controls for the live broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newscast schedule and strict timing constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 44 newscasts every weekday and 24 on the weekend; the newscasts always run on the hour for five minutes, with additional shorter newscasts at set times during Morning Edition and All Things Considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchors 'have to be off the air on the exact second' so member stations and programs can continue; producers and anchors must manage pacing, stretch or compress copy (e.g., slowing pace or adding stock updates) to hit time precisely. Member stations may cut into the newscast after three minutes for local news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story selection philosophy: relevancy and immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about blocking a newscast are generally based on two main factors: relevancy to the lives of our listeners and immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A breaking or immediate story may lead briefly; other major stories can dominate for hours or days (e.g., terrorist attacks, severe weather). Consumer/business or health stories are good leads when they impact finances or physical well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for stories with national appeal (avoid being too local)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, we want to use stories that will have national appeal and unless they are spectacular or unique, we won't get too local.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local items may be excluded unless they are spectacular/unique; this aligns with the national distribution of newscasts across ~780 member stations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid duplication with newsmagazines and coordinate correspondent voices
rubrics_metrics.description: The newscasts team looks at what stories are coming up on the newsmagazines so that it doesn't duplicate stories or correspondent voices too close to when they air on the program itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes duplication is unavoidable during big breaking stories, but producers will try to adjust the schedule so listeners don't immediately hear the same correspondent reporting on both the newscast and the newsmagazine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of themes and grouping of stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Newscasts often contain themes, so there is a tendency to group stories together that have commonality — crime stories, business stories, political stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grouping creates coherent short packages for the listener and can inform ordering decisions within a five-minute block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: focus on breaking news and big items; leave features to newsmagazines
rubrics_metrics.description: The newscasts primarily cover breaking news and the big news items of the day, and leave the features, trend stories and long interviews to the newsmagazines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This scope helps preserve the short, immediate nature of newscasts and avoids overlap with long-form programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition policy and rules for re-airing reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a story airs during one broadcast, the news cycle will determine whether it will air again during another broadcast. The team might broadcast a particular report a few different times to make sure the most listeners hear it, depending on its importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an operational preference for at least two, and more often three, hours of separation using the same correspondent report. They generally do not run more than twice (or avoid excessive repetition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness must be evident in each and every newscast
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers and anchors are asked to assume that the newscast listeners are hearing the next hour is the only one they will hear that day; the fairness standard must be evident in each and every newscast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During campaign coverage the team will try to speak about both candidates in the same broadcast and alternates which candidate gets first billing across successive newscasts to avoid perceived bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking and sourcing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The newscasts team says it aggressively fact-checks everything; they will sacrifice a story in the lineup if it does not have confirmation from two sources, and, in the case of major news, a sign-off from a top editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocols were tightened after prior errors (e.g., incorrect Giffords death report); for sensitive items like Cabinet nominations the team tries to independently confirm every nomination and will wait hours if necessary to get confirmations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections policy for on-air errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The newscasts make relatively few errors that require a correction, but they will issue an on-air correction when they do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant errors (e.g., hoaxes that were widely reported) are corrected on-air in a later broadcast. Smaller mistakes like mispronunciations or partial misidentifications are corrected internally so they are not repeated but typically will not merit an on-air correction or explanation; there are no archived transcripts to append written corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live designation: newscasts are identified as 'live'
rubrics_metrics.description: Newscasts begin with a note that the show is 'live' — a deliberate choice made earlier in the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The live label signals immediacy and the fact that anchors are performing/engineering in real time; it addresses listener questions about format changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formats and lengths: reported vs. anchor-read pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: The elements of a newscast are either read by the anchor live, or are recordings from a reporter with a live introduction from the anchor. Reported stories are usually around 40-45 seconds long, while stories read by the anchor range in length but are usually shorter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archived audio from an event or person can be played in either format. Producers must craft or choose audio to fit the fixed time windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Member station practices and variability in what listeners hear
rubrics_metrics.description: The vast majority of NPR's member stations subscribe to the newscasts, but listeners may only hear the newscasts at the top of the hour depending on their member station. Member stations may also cut into the newscasts after three minutes during the broadcast at the top of the hour to make time for local news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of station-level differences and listener tuning behavior, the newscast team considers distribution variability in deciding repetition and which stories to push.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing and continuous operation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The newscasts team is the only broadcast unit at NPR that works 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year; at least three of the team's 27 full-time employees (along with temporary workers) are always on duty preparing newscasts at least every hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous operation requires staffing plans that cover production, editing, and fact-checking for every shift and hour.
